{"answer": "## Repeatable Manipulation Benchmarks for Comparing Low-Cost and Industrial/Research Robot Arms

This report identifies published manipulation benchmarks with quantitative results obtained on industrial or research arms that could be rerun on a low-cost 6-DOF arm (such as AgileX PiPER or SO-101) equipped with a parallel gripper and RGB cameras. For each benchmark, the protocol, trial count, success criterion, measuring tool, arm model, and key quantitative result are described. The following table provides a comprehensive summary of all identified benchmarks.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

### 1. ISO 9283 Pose Repeatability and Accuracy

**Protocol.** The ISO 9283:1998 standard prescribes approaching each of five target poses arranged in an ISO cube configuration 30 times from the same direction. The end-effector position is recorded at each arrival, and positional repeatability is computed as the mean three-dimensional radial deviation plus three standard deviations (RPₗ = l̄ + 3σ) (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000003). Testing is performed unloaded and with a specified payload. Pose accuracy is the deviation between the commanded and measured mean positions.

**Published results.** On an RTA ARTIC6-1215-6kg, the contact-based unloaded test yielded 0.0260 mm repeatability over 30 cycles using three orthogonal digital dial indicators; the vision-based test with a 4 kg payload yielded 0.0406 mm using a calibrated OptiTrack multi-camera system (pqac-00000001). At the five ISO cube points with payload, repeatability ranged from 0.02691 mm to 0.26279 mm (pqac-00000001). Kirschner et al. extended the ISO 9283 framework to force-sensing and safety benchmarking on a Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, and UR10e (DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329), though positional repeatability in millimeters was not separately reported in the retrieved text (pqac-00000005). Pollák et al. (2020) reported unidirectional pose accuracy and repeatability of the collaborative UR5 per ISO 9283 (DOI: 10.1177/1687814020972893), but the full text was unobtainable (pqac-00000006).

**Replication on low-cost arms.** This test requires only a rigid end-effector tool, a measuring instrument (dial indicators or an external camera system such as OptiTrack or even ArUco/AprilTag tracking with a calibrated external camera), and programmed motion to fixed targets. A low-cost arm can run the same 30-cycle protocol. **No published ISO 9283 result exists for the PiPER or SO-101.**

---

### 2. Box and Blocks Test (BBT)

**Protocol.** Morgan et al. (2020) adapted the clinical Box and Blocks Test into three robot protocols using the YCB apparatus (objects #68 and #69). The Modified-BBT requires transferring 16 aligned blocks over a barrier. The Targeted-BBT adds ordered placement accuracy. The Standard-BBT transfers as many randomly configured blocks as possible, with a timed (60 s) and untimed variant. Each protocol is run consecutively at least five times; a failed execution scores zero (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022).

**Published results on Franka Panda.** Modified-BBT: average score 14.40, total time 247.94 s. Targeted-BBT: score 13.00, total time 307.10 s. Timed Standard-BBT: 2.80 blocks in 60 s. Untimed Standard-BBT: 7.60 blocks in 248.73 s. The Panda used an extended parallel gripper (140 mm 3D-printed fingertips) and an Intel RealSense D435i eye-in-hand sensor (pqac-00000018). A Barrett WAM with a Yale Openhand T42 gripper outperformed the Panda, transferring an average of 4.8 ± 0.4 blocks in the untimed variant (pqac-00000017). DOI: 10.1109/LRA.2019.2961053 (peer-reviewed, IEEE RA-L).

**Replication.** The BBT apparatus is commercially available and 3D-printable. A low-cost arm with a parallel gripper and wrist camera can directly replicate this benchmark, measuring blocks transferred and time.

---

### 3. NIST Assembly Task Board — Peg-in-Hole and Connector Insertion

**Protocol.** Kimble et al. (2020) defined a standardized benchmarking protocol using NIST Assembly Task Boards. Task Board 1 includes four round pegs (4, 8, 12, 16 mm diameter), four rectangular pegs, four connectors (USB, RJ45, waterproof, DSUB), gears, and fasteners. In the assembly mode, a fully disassembled board and parts kit are placed within the robot's work volume; the robot autonomously grasps each part and assembles it. Performance is evaluated using completion time, board completion percentage, and reliability (probability of successful sub-task completion). Mean, standard deviation, and 95% confidence interval are required over trials (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000014). DOI: 10.1109/LRA.2020.2965869 (peer-reviewed, IEEE RA-L, 157 citations).

**Published results.** Lian et al. (2021) benchmarked off-the-shelf solutions on a UR5e using a subset of NIST Task Board 1. With a 3D-vision system (two LMI Gocator 3506 sensors), 150 trials per task were conducted: all peg tasks and most connectors achieved 100% completion except for four RJ45 failures (pqac-00000043). End-to-end connector insertion results: USB 100.0% / 29.8 s mean cycle time; RJ45 96.0% / 33.6 s; waterproof 98.0% / 30.1 s; DSUB 100.0% / 28.0 s (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000065). DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636586 (peer-reviewed, IROS 2021).

**Replication.** The NIST task board designs use standard off-the-shelf components and are publicly documented. A low-cost arm can attempt the same peg insertions and connector tasks, though tight-clearance connectors may exceed the positional accuracy of budget hardware.

---

### 4. Peg-in-Hole with Controlled Positional Error

**Protocol.** Van Wyk et al. (2018) defined a comparative peg-in-hole benchmark using 3D-printable pegs and holes with a dimensionless clearance of c = (D − d)/D = 0.02. Each test involves 60 attempted insertions with deliberate Gaussian positional offsets (σ = 1 mm and 2 mm). Completion time (CT) measures only the alignment-to-insertion phase, excluding peg acquisition and transport. Probability of success (PS) is calculated with 95% confidence (pqac-00000042). DOI: 10.1109/TRO.2018.2791591 (peer-reviewed, IEEE Transactions on Robotics, 138 citations).

**Published results.** At σ₁ = 1 mm offset: System 1 (conventional gripper) achieved PS = 85.4%, mean CT = 11.70 s; System 2 Quasi-Random (force-controlled hand) achieved PS = 95.2%, mean CT = 3.11 s. At σ₂ = 2 mm offset: System 1 achieved PS = 87.6%, mean CT = 18.31 s; System 2 Quasi-Random achieved PS = 95.2%, mean CT = 8.2 s (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064).

**Replication.** The 3D-printable test artifacts make this highly accessible. A low-cost arm can run the same 60-insertion protocol with known offsets, measuring success and insertion time.

---

### 5. QBIT — Quality-Aware Benchmarking for Robotic Insertion Tasks

**Protocol.** Schempp et al. (2025) introduced QBIT, evaluating position-controlled, force-controlled, and learning-based (InsertionNet) insertion approaches on a UR5e with a six-axis force/torque sensor. Peg-in-hole scenarios used 1 mm and 0.1 mm clearances plus USB-plug insertion. Metrics include success rate, force energy, force smoothness, and completion time, calculated from 100 repetitions per approach (pqac-00000041). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2503.07479 (**preprint**, arXiv 2025).

**Replication.** The protocol requires a force/torque sensor for full quality metrics, but success rate and completion time alone can be measured with a low-cost arm and video scoring.

---

### 6. YCB Object Pick-and-Place — SceneReplica

**Protocol.** Khargonkar et al. (2024) created 20 reproducible tabletop scenes, each containing five objects from a set of 16 YCB objects. The robot attempts grasp, lift, rotate, transport, and drop-off. Both grasping success and complete pick-and-place success are scored separately over 100 object attempts per pipeline (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000069).

**Published results on Fetch robot.** Success rates ranged from 36% to 66% depending on the perception and grasp-planning pipeline. The best non-oracle result was GDRNPP + GraspIt! top-down grasping at 66/100 (66%). Ground-truth-pose variants reached 78–82/100 (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000068). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10610180 (peer-reviewed, ICRA 2024).

**Replication.** The YCB object set is commercially available. Scene layouts are specified with stencils. A low-cost arm with an RGB camera can replicate this, substituting its own perception pipeline.

---

### 7. ACRV Picking Benchmark

**Protocol.** Leitner et al. (2017) designed a reproducible shelf-picking benchmark with 42 common objects, a widely available shelf, and exact arrangement stencils. Four setups of increasing difficulty are each run three consecutive times. Success rate = successful picks / attempted picks (pqac-00000021). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2017.7989545 (peer-reviewed, ICRA 2017, 110 citations).

**Published results on Baxter.** Setup 1: 75% (9/12); Setup 2: 33.33% (4/12); Setup 3: 8.33% (1/12); Setup 4: 0% (0/18) (pqac-00000021).

**Replication.** The shelf and object arrangement are reproducible by design. A parallel gripper can substitute for the vacuum end-effector used on Baxter, though success rates will differ.

---

### 8. FMB — Functional Manipulation Benchmark

**Protocol.** Luo et al. (2024) proposed FMB using a Franka Panda with torque control. It evaluates grasping (5 trials × 10 objects = 50), single-object long-horizon manipulation (30 trials), and multi-object assembly (10 trials) using 66 reproducible 3D-printed objects. Observations include multi-camera RGB-D, kinematics, and force/torque (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038).

**Published results.** Grasping: Transformer policy 28/50 (56%), ResNet 27/50 (54%). Single-object assembly: best 19/30. Multi-object assembly: best 7/10 (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). DOI: 10.1177/02783649241276017 (peer-reviewed, IJRR 2024, 161 citations).

**Replication.** The 3D-printed objects and CAD files are publicly available. A low-cost arm can attempt the grasping and single-object assembly tasks; multi-object assembly may require force sensing not available on budget platforms.

---

### 9. FurnitureBench

**Protocol.** Heo et al. (2025) evaluated long-horizon furniture assembly on a Franka Panda with the default parallel gripper and three Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D cameras. Eight 3D-printable furniture models test grasping, insertion, screwing, and pushing. Individual skills are evaluated over 10 trials under low/medium initialization randomness; termination occurs on completion, 5 s inactivity, unsafe motion, or step limits (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033). DOI: 10.1177/02783649241304789 (peer-reviewed, IJRR 2025, 241 citations).

**Published results.** Individual skill success rates vary by part and randomness. Full-assembly learning methods averaged at most 2 of 12 subtasks. Rebuilt environments achieved 84% of original one-leg-task phase performance (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034).

**Replication.** The 3D-printable models are available. Single-skill tasks (grasp, insert) are feasible on low-cost arms, though full assembly may exceed their capabilities.

---

### 10. Low-Cost Arm Benchmarks: SO-100/SO-101 with LeRobot

**SmolVLA on SO-100.** Shukor et al. (2025) evaluated ACT, SmolVLA, and π0 on three SO-100 tasks (pick-place, stacking, sorting) using 50 demonstrations per task. ACT achieved 70%/50%/25% (mean 48.3%); SmolVLA achieved 75%/90%/70% (mean 78.3%); π0 achieved 100%/40%/45% (mean 61.7%) (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2506.01844 (**preprint**, arXiv 2025, 655 citations).

**Cowling SO-101 scaling study.** Cowling (2026) compared ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0.5 on an SO-101 green-ball pick-and-place task with two distractors, using nested demonstration sets of 12–200. Each evaluation block ran 10 fixed placements with a 30 s timeout. Over 1,340 scored episodes, ACT improved from 1/40 at 12 demonstrations to 37/40 at 100; π0.5 achieved 16/40 at 12 and ~70% at higher counts; SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peaked near 50% (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.37170 (**preprint**, arXiv 2026).

**SO-101 Bench.** Hickok (2026) defined a language-conditioned spatial manipulation benchmark with Bin, Next-to, Between, and Move tasks across 916 simulated episodes and 60 paired physical episodes. Learned policies ranged from 8% to 60.8%; the best agent+grasp combination reached 83.2% in simulation (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.36420 (**preprint**, arXiv 2026).

---

### 11. Laboratory Manipulation Tasks

**MATTERIX.** Darvish et al. (2025) used a Franka Research 3 for lab tasks: beaker pick-and-place achieved 9/12 (75%) success; liquid pouring achieved 9/10 (90%) with 59.6 ± 7.9 mL transferred (pqac-00000055). DOI: 10.1038/s43588-025-00924-4 (peer-reviewed, Nature Computational Science 2025).

**Mobile robot rack handling.** Burger (2023) reported 464/464 (100%) rack transfers using a KUKA LBR iiwa arm with a Festo parallel gripper over 71 iterations in a 2-hour robustness test (pqac-00000050). DOI: 10.17638/03087073.

**ABB YuMi vial handling.** Manna et al. (2026) used an ABB YuMi IRB 14000 for end-to-end Drosophila vial handling, achieving 93.85% retention of flies fit for analysis across 1,024 assays versus 83.33% for a human (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000052). DOI: 10.64898/2026.10.20.758951 (**preprint**, bioRxiv 2026).

**No published evidence was found for a standardized, repeatable vial-into-rack insertion benchmark with trial-level success rates on any industrial arm.** This remains a gap in the literature.

---

### Summary and Gaps

The benchmarks most immediately replicable on a low-cost arm with a parallel gripper and RGB cameras are: (1) ISO 9283-style pose repeatability using AprilTag tracking in lieu of an OptiTrack system; (2) the Box and Blocks Test with the YCB apparatus; (3) YCB object pick-and-place following SceneReplica scenes; (4) NIST task board peg insertions (especially the larger pegs); (5) SO-100/SO-101 LeRobot tasks (pick-place, stacking, sorting), which are already native to the user's platform; and (6) the Van Wyk peg-in-hole protocol with 3D-printed artifacts.

**Explicit gaps.** No peer-reviewed ISO 9283 positional repeatability values were found for the AgileX PiPER or SO-101. No standardized vial-into-rack benchmark with published trial-level success rates exists. The QBIT and FMB force-based quality metrics require a force/torque sensor not present on budget arms. The Kinova Gen3 and ABB YuMi lack published results on the NIST task board or BBT benchmarks in the retrieved literature, limiting direct cross-arm comparisons for those specific platforms."}

## Repeatable Manipulation Benchmarks for Comparing Low-Cost and Industrial/Research Robot Arms

This report identifies published manipulation benchmarks with quantitative results obtained on industrial or research arms that could be rerun on a low-cost 6-DOF arm (such as AgileX PiPER or SO-101) equipped with a parallel gripper and RGB cameras. For each benchmark, the protocol, trial count, success criterion, measuring tool, arm model, and key quantitative result are described. ### 1. ISO 9283 Pose Repeatability and Accuracy

**Protocol.** The ISO 9283:1998 standard prescribes approaching each of five target poses arranged in an ISO cube configuration 30 times from the same direction. The end-effector position is recorded at each arrival, and positional repeatability is computed as the mean three-dimensional radial deviation plus three standard deviations (RPₗ = l̄ + 3σ) (nasertorabi2024repeatabilityassessmentof pages 7-10, nasertorabi2024repeatabilityassessmentof pages 1-4). Testing is performed unloaded and with a specified payload. Pose accuracy is the deviation between the commanded and measured mean positions.

**Published results.** On an RTA ARTIC6-1215-6kg, the contact-based unloaded test yielded 0.0260 mm repeatability over 30 cycles using three orthogonal digital dial indicators; the vision-based test with a 4 kg payload yielded 0.0406 mm using a calibrated OptiTrack multi-camera system (nasertorabi2024repeatabilityassessmentof pages 24-26). At the five ISO cube points with payload, repeatability ranged from 0.02691 mm to 0.26279 mm (nasertorabi2024repeatabilityassessmentof pages 24-26). Kirschner et al. extended the ISO 9283 framework to force-sensing and safety benchmarking on a Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, and UR10e (DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329), though positional repeatability in millimeters was not separately reported in the retrieved text (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 2-3). Pollák et al. (2020) reported unidirectional pose accuracy and repeatability of the collaborative UR5 per ISO 9283 (DOI: 10.1177/1687814020972893), but the full text was unobtainable (nasertorabi2024repeatabilityassessmentof pages 44-45).

**Replication on low-cost arms.** This test requires only a rigid end-effector tool, a measuring instrument (dial indicators or an external camera system such as OptiTrack or even ArUco/AprilTag tracking with a calibrated external camera), and programmed motion to fixed targets. A low-cost arm can run the same 30-cycle protocol. **No published ISO 9283 result exists for the PiPER or SO-101.**

### 2. Box and Blocks Test (BBT)

**Protocol.** Morgan et al. (2020) adapted the clinical Box and Blocks Test into three robot protocols using the YCB apparatus (objects #68 and #69). The Modified-BBT requires transferring 16 aligned blocks over a barrier. The Targeted-BBT adds ordered placement accuracy. The Standard-BBT transfers as many randomly configured blocks as possible, with a timed (60 s) and untimed variant. Each protocol is run consecutively at least five times; a failed execution scores zero (morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 2-3, morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 4-5).

**Published results on Franka Panda.** Modified-BBT: average score 14.40, total time 247.94 s. Targeted-BBT: score 13.00, total time 307.10 s. Timed Standard-BBT: 2.80 blocks in 60 s. Untimed Standard-BBT: 7.60 blocks in 248.73 s. The Panda used an extended parallel gripper (140 mm 3D-printed fingertips) and an Intel RealSense D435i eye-in-hand sensor (morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 5-6). A Barrett WAM with a Yale Openhand T42 gripper outperformed the Panda, transferring an average of 4.8 ± 0.4 blocks in the untimed variant (morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 7-8). DOI: 10.1109/LRA.2019.2961053 (peer-reviewed, IEEE RA-L).

**Replication.** The BBT apparatus is commercially available and 3D-printable. A low-cost arm with a parallel gripper and wrist camera can directly replicate this benchmark, measuring blocks transferred and time.

### 3. NIST Assembly Task Board — Peg-in-Hole and Connector Insertion

**Protocol.** Kimble et al. (2020) defined a standardized benchmarking protocol using NIST Assembly Task Boards. Task Board 1 includes four round pegs (4, 8, 12, 16 mm diameter), four rectangular pegs, four connectors (USB, RJ45, waterproof, DSUB), gears, and fasteners. In the assembly mode, a fully disassembled board and parts kit are placed within the robot's work volume; the robot autonomously grasps each part and assembles it. Performance is evaluated using completion time, board completion percentage, and reliability (probability of successful sub-task completion). Mean, standard deviation, and 95% confidence interval are required over trials (kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 6-9, kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 3-5). DOI: 10.1109/LRA.2020.2965869 (peer-reviewed, IEEE RA-L, 157 citations).

**Published results.** Lian et al. (2021) benchmarked off-the-shelf solutions on a UR5e using a subset of NIST Task Board 1. With a 3D-vision system (two LMI Gocator 3506 sensors), 150 trials per task were conducted: all peg tasks and most connectors achieved 100% completion except for four RJ45 failures (lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 4-5). End-to-end connector insertion results: USB 100.0% / 29.8 s mean cycle time; RJ45 96.0% / 33.6 s; waterproof 98.0% / 30.1 s; DSUB 100.0% / 28.0 s (lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 7-7, lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions media c9397f47). DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636586 (peer-reviewed, IROS 2021).

**Replication.** The NIST task board designs use standard off-the-shelf components and are publicly documented. A low-cost arm can attempt the same peg insertions and connector tasks, though tight-clearance connectors may exceed the positional accuracy of budget hardware.

### 4. Peg-in-Hole with Controlled Positional Error

**Protocol.** Van Wyk et al. (2018) defined a comparative peg-in-hole benchmark using 3D-printable pegs and holes with a dimensionless clearance of c = (D − d)/D = 0.02. Each test involves 60 attempted insertions with deliberate Gaussian positional offsets (σ = 1 mm and 2 mm). Completion time (CT) measures only the alignment-to-insertion phase, excluding peg acquisition and transport. Probability of success (PS) is calculated with 95% confidence (wyk2018comparativepeginholetesting pages 3-5). DOI: 10.1109/TRO.2018.2791591 (peer-reviewed, IEEE Transactions on Robotics, 138 citations).

**Published results.** At σ₁ = 1 mm offset: System 1 (conventional gripper) achieved PS = 85.4%, mean CT = 11.70 s; System 2 Quasi-Random (force-controlled hand) achieved PS = 95.2%, mean CT = 3.11 s. At σ₂ = 2 mm offset: System 1 achieved PS = 87.6%, mean CT = 18.31 s; System 2 Quasi-Random achieved PS = 95.2%, mean CT = 8.2 s (wyk2018comparativepeginholetesting media eff4b610, wyk2018comparativepeginholetesting media 139c342d).

**Replication.** The 3D-printable test artifacts make this highly accessible. A low-cost arm can run the same 60-insertion protocol with known offsets, measuring success and insertion time.

### 5. QBIT — Quality-Aware Benchmarking for Robotic Insertion Tasks

**Protocol.** Schempp et al. (2025) introduced QBIT, evaluating position-controlled, force-controlled, and learning-based (InsertionNet) insertion approaches on a UR5e with a six-axis force/torque sensor. Peg-in-hole scenarios used 1 mm and 0.1 mm clearances plus USB-plug insertion. Metrics include success rate, force energy, force smoothness, and completion time, calculated from 100 repetitions per approach (schempp2025qbitqualityawarecloudbased pages 4-5). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2503.07479 (**preprint**, arXiv 2025).

**Replication.** The protocol requires a force/torque sensor for full quality metrics, but success rate and completion time alone can be measured with a low-cost arm and video scoring.

### 6. YCB Object Pick-and-Place — SceneReplica

**Protocol.** Khargonkar et al. (2024) created 20 reproducible tabletop scenes, each containing five objects from a set of 16 YCB objects. The robot attempts grasp, lift, rotate, transport, and drop-off. Both grasping success and complete pick-and-place success are scored separately over 100 object attempts per pipeline (khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 9-11, khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 3-5).

**Published results on Fetch robot.** Success rates ranged from 36% to 66% depending on the perception and grasp-planning pipeline. The best non-oracle result was GDRNPP + GraspIt! top-down grasping at 66/100 (66%). Ground-truth-pose variants reached 78–82/100 (khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 9-11, khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 6-7, khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 5-6). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10610180 (peer-reviewed, ICRA 2024).

**Replication.** The YCB object set is commercially available. Scene layouts are specified with stencils. A low-cost arm with an RGB camera can replicate this, substituting its own perception pipeline.

### 7. ACRV Picking Benchmark

**Protocol.** Leitner et al. (2017) designed a reproducible shelf-picking benchmark with 42 common objects, a widely available shelf, and exact arrangement stencils. Four setups of increasing difficulty are each run three consecutive times. Success rate = successful picks / attempted picks (leitner2017theacrvpicking pages 7-7). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2017.7989545 (peer-reviewed, ICRA 2017, 110 citations).

**Published results on Baxter.** Setup 1: 75% (9/12); Setup 2: 33.33% (4/12); Setup 3: 8.33% (1/12); Setup 4: 0% (0/18) (leitner2017theacrvpicking pages 7-7).

**Replication.** The shelf and object arrangement are reproducible by design. A parallel gripper can substitute for the vacuum end-effector used on Baxter, though success rates will differ.

### 8. FMB — Functional Manipulation Benchmark

**Protocol.** Luo et al. (2024) proposed FMB using a Franka Panda with torque control. It evaluates grasping (5 trials × 10 objects = 50), single-object long-horizon manipulation (30 trials), and multi-object assembly (10 trials) using 66 reproducible 3D-printed objects. Observations include multi-camera RGB-D, kinematics, and force/torque (luo2025fmbafunctional pages 5-7, luo2025fmbafunctional pages 9-11).

**Published results.** Grasping: Transformer policy 28/50 (56%), ResNet 27/50 (54%). Single-object assembly: best 19/30. Multi-object assembly: best 7/10 (luo2025fmbafunctional pages 14-15, luo2025fmbafunctional pages 9-11). DOI: 10.1177/02783649241276017 (peer-reviewed, IJRR 2024, 161 citations).

**Replication.** The 3D-printed objects and CAD files are publicly available. A low-cost arm can attempt the grasping and single-object assembly tasks; multi-object assembly may require force sensing not available on budget platforms.

### 9. FurnitureBench

**Protocol.** Heo et al. (2025) evaluated long-horizon furniture assembly on a Franka Panda with the default parallel gripper and three Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D cameras. Eight 3D-printable furniture models test grasping, insertion, screwing, and pushing. Individual skills are evaluated over 10 trials under low/medium initialization randomness; termination occurs on completion, 5 s inactivity, unsafe motion, or step limits (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 3-4, heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 6-7). DOI: 10.1177/02783649241304789 (peer-reviewed, IJRR 2025, 241 citations).

**Published results.** Individual skill success rates vary by part and randomness. Full-assembly learning methods averaged at most 2 of 12 subtasks. Rebuilt environments achieved 84% of original one-leg-task phase performance (heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 3-4, heo2025furniturebenchreproduciblerealworld pages 1-2).

**Replication.** The 3D-printable models are available. Single-skill tasks (grasp, insert) are feasible on low-cost arms, though full assembly may exceed their capabilities.

### 10. Low-Cost Arm Benchmarks: SO-100/SO-101 with LeRobot

**SmolVLA on SO-100.** Shukor et al. (2025) evaluated ACT, SmolVLA, and π0 on three SO-100 tasks (pick-place, stacking, sorting) using 50 demonstrations per task. ACT achieved 70%/50%/25% (mean 48.3%); SmolVLA achieved 75%/90%/70% (mean 78.3%); π0 achieved 100%/40%/45% (mean 61.7%) (shukor2025smolvlaavisionlanguageaction pages 10-12, shukor2025smolvlaavisionlanguageaction pages 12-14). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2506.01844 (**preprint**, arXiv 2025, 655 citations).

**Cowling SO-101 scaling study.** Cowling (2026) compared ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0.5 on an SO-101 green-ball pick-and-place task with two distractors, using nested demonstration sets of 12–200. Each evaluation block ran 10 fixed placements with a 30 s timeout. Over 1,340 scored episodes, ACT improved from 1/40 at 12 demonstrations to 37/40 at 100; π0.5 achieved 16/40 at 12 and ~70% at higher counts; SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peaked near 50% (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3, cowling2026from12to pages 7-9, cowling2026from12to pages 3-5). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.37170 (**preprint**, arXiv 2026).

**SO-101 Bench.** Hickok (2026) defined a language-conditioned spatial manipulation benchmark with Bin, Next-to, Between, and Move tasks across 916 simulated episodes and 60 paired physical episodes. Learned policies ranged from 8% to 60.8%; the best agent+grasp combination reached 83.2% in simulation (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 13-16, hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 2-4, hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 1-2). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.36420 (**preprint**, arXiv 2026).

### 11. Laboratory Manipulation Tasks

**MATTERIX.** Darvish et al. (2025) used a Franka Research 3 for lab tasks: beaker pick-and-place achieved 9/12 (75%) success; liquid pouring achieved 9/10 (90%) with 59.6 ± 7.9 mL transferred (darvish2025matterixtowarda pages 11-14). DOI: 10.1038/s43588-025-00924-4 (peer-reviewed, Nature Computational Science 2025).

**Mobile robot rack handling.** Burger (2023) reported 464/464 (100%) rack transfers using a KUKA LBR iiwa arm with a Festo parallel gripper over 71 iterations in a 2-hour robustness test (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 62-69). DOI: 10.17638/03087073.

**ABB YuMi vial handling.** Manna et al. (2026) used an ABB YuMi IRB 14000 for end-to-end Drosophila vial handling, achieving 93.85% retention of flies fit for analysis across 1,024 assays versus 83.33% for a human (manna2026endtoendautomationof pages 1-3, manna2026endtoendautomationof pages 3-5). DOI: 10.64898/2026.10.20.758951 (**preprint**, bioRxiv 2026).

**No published evidence was found for a standardized, repeatable vial-into-rack insertion benchmark with trial-level success rates on any industrial arm.** This remains a gap in the literature.

---

### Summary and Gaps

The benchmarks most immediately replicable on a low-cost arm with a parallel gripper and RGB cameras are: (1) ISO 9283-style pose repeatability using AprilTag tracking in lieu of an OptiTrack system; (2) the Box and Blocks Test with the YCB apparatus; (3) YCB object pick-and-place following SceneReplica scenes; (4) NIST task board peg insertions (especially the larger pegs); (5) SO-100/SO-101 LeRobot tasks (pick-place, stacking, sorting), which are already native to the user's platform; and (6) the Van Wyk peg-in-hole protocol with 3D-printed artifacts.

**Explicit gaps.** No peer-reviewed ISO 9283 positional repeatability values were found for the AgileX PiPER or SO-101. No standardized vial-into-rack benchmark with published trial-level success rates exists. The QBIT and FMB force-based quality metrics require a force/torque sensor not present on budget arms. The Kinova Gen3 and ABB YuMi lack published results on the NIST task board or BBT benchmarks in the retrieved literature, limiting direct cross-arm comparisons for those specific platforms.

*Table: Published and preprint benchmarks that can be adapted to a low-cost parallel-gripper arm with RGB cameras. The table separates reproducible protocols and verified quantitative baselines from cases where the literature does not publish sufficient trial-level evidence.*

---

### 1. ISO 9283 Pose Repeatability and Accuracy

**Protocol.** The ISO 9283:1998 standard prescribes approaching each of five target poses arranged in an ISO cube configuration 30 times from the same direction. The end-effector position is recorded at each arrival, and positional repeatability is computed as the mean three-dimensional radial deviation plus three standard deviations (RPₗ = l̄ + 3σ) (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000003). Testing is performed unloaded and with a specified payload. Pose accuracy is the deviation between the commanded and measured mean positions.

**Published results.** On an RTA ARTIC6-1215-6kg, the contact-based unloaded test yielded 0.0260 mm repeatability over 30 cycles using three orthogonal digital dial indicators; the vision-based test with a 4 kg payload yielded 0.0406 mm using a calibrated OptiTrack multi-camera system (pqac-00000001). At the five ISO cube points with payload, repeatability ranged from 0.02691 mm to 0.26279 mm (pqac-00000001). Kirschner et al. extended the ISO 9283 framework to force-sensing and safety benchmarking on a Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, and UR10e (DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329), though positional repeatability in millimeters was not separately reported in the retrieved text (pqac-00000005). Pollák et al. (2020) reported unidirectional pose accuracy and repeatability of the collaborative UR5 per ISO 9283 (DOI: 10.1177/1687814020972893), but the full text was unobtainable (pqac-00000006).

**Replication on low-cost arms.** This test requires only a rigid end-effector tool, a measuring instrument (dial indicators or an external camera system such as OptiTrack or even ArUco/AprilTag tracking with a calibrated external camera), and programmed motion to fixed targets. A low-cost arm can run the same 30-cycle protocol. **No published ISO 9283 result exists for the PiPER or SO-101.**

---

### 2. Box and Blocks Test (BBT)

**Protocol.** Morgan et al. (2020) adapted the clinical Box and Blocks Test into three robot protocols using the YCB apparatus (objects #68 and #69). The Modified-BBT requires transferring 16 aligned blocks over a barrier. The Targeted-BBT adds ordered placement accuracy. The Standard-BBT transfers as many randomly configured blocks as possible, with a timed (60 s) and untimed variant. Each protocol is run consecutively at least five times; a failed execution scores zero (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000022).

**Published results on Franka Panda.** Modified-BBT: average score 14.40, total time 247.94 s. Targeted-BBT: score 13.00, total time 307.10 s. Timed Standard-BBT: 2.80 blocks in 60 s. Untimed Standard-BBT: 7.60 blocks in 248.73 s. The Panda used an extended parallel gripper (140 mm 3D-printed fingertips) and an Intel RealSense D435i eye-in-hand sensor (pqac-00000018). A Barrett WAM with a Yale Openhand T42 gripper outperformed the Panda, transferring an average of 4.8 ± 0.4 blocks in the untimed variant (pqac-00000017). DOI: 10.1109/LRA.2019.2961053 (peer-reviewed, IEEE RA-L).

**Replication.** The BBT apparatus is commercially available and 3D-printable. A low-cost arm with a parallel gripper and wrist camera can directly replicate this benchmark, measuring blocks transferred and time.

---

### 3. NIST Assembly Task Board — Peg-in-Hole and Connector Insertion

**Protocol.** Kimble et al. (2020) defined a standardized benchmarking protocol using NIST Assembly Task Boards. Task Board 1 includes four round pegs (4, 8, 12, 16 mm diameter), four rectangular pegs, four connectors (USB, RJ45, waterproof, DSUB), gears, and fasteners. In the assembly mode, a fully disassembled board and parts kit are placed within the robot's work volume; the robot autonomously grasps each part and assembles it. Performance is evaluated using completion time, board completion percentage, and reliability (probability of successful sub-task completion). Mean, standard deviation, and 95% confidence interval are required over trials (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000014). DOI: 10.1109/LRA.2020.2965869 (peer-reviewed, IEEE RA-L, 157 citations).

**Published results.** Lian et al. (2021) benchmarked off-the-shelf solutions on a UR5e using a subset of NIST Task Board 1. With a 3D-vision system (two LMI Gocator 3506 sensors), 150 trials per task were conducted: all peg tasks and most connectors achieved 100% completion except for four RJ45 failures (pqac-00000043). End-to-end connector insertion results: USB 100.0% / 29.8 s mean cycle time; RJ45 96.0% / 33.6 s; waterproof 98.0% / 30.1 s; DSUB 100.0% / 28.0 s (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000065). DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636586 (peer-reviewed, IROS 2021).

**Replication.** The NIST task board designs use standard off-the-shelf components and are publicly documented. A low-cost arm can attempt the same peg insertions and connector tasks, though tight-clearance connectors may exceed the positional accuracy of budget hardware.

---

### 4. Peg-in-Hole with Controlled Positional Error

**Protocol.** Van Wyk et al. (2018) defined a comparative peg-in-hole benchmark using 3D-printable pegs and holes with a dimensionless clearance of c = (D − d)/D = 0.02. Each test involves 60 attempted insertions with deliberate Gaussian positional offsets (σ = 1 mm and 2 mm). Completion time (CT) measures only the alignment-to-insertion phase, excluding peg acquisition and transport. Probability of success (PS) is calculated with 95% confidence (pqac-00000042). DOI: 10.1109/TRO.2018.2791591 (peer-reviewed, IEEE Transactions on Robotics, 138 citations).

**Published results.** At σ₁ = 1 mm offset: System 1 (conventional gripper) achieved PS = 85.4%, mean CT = 11.70 s; System 2 Quasi-Random (force-controlled hand) achieved PS = 95.2%, mean CT = 3.11 s. At σ₂ = 2 mm offset: System 1 achieved PS = 87.6%, mean CT = 18.31 s; System 2 Quasi-Random achieved PS = 95.2%, mean CT = 8.2 s (pqac-00000062, pqac-00000064).

**Replication.** The 3D-printable test artifacts make this highly accessible. A low-cost arm can run the same 60-insertion protocol with known offsets, measuring success and insertion time.

---

### 5. QBIT — Quality-Aware Benchmarking for Robotic Insertion Tasks

**Protocol.** Schempp et al. (2025) introduced QBIT, evaluating position-controlled, force-controlled, and learning-based (InsertionNet) insertion approaches on a UR5e with a six-axis force/torque sensor. Peg-in-hole scenarios used 1 mm and 0.1 mm clearances plus USB-plug insertion. Metrics include success rate, force energy, force smoothness, and completion time, calculated from 100 repetitions per approach (pqac-00000041). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2503.07479 (**preprint**, arXiv 2025).

**Replication.** The protocol requires a force/torque sensor for full quality metrics, but success rate and completion time alone can be measured with a low-cost arm and video scoring.

---

### 6. YCB Object Pick-and-Place — SceneReplica

**Protocol.** Khargonkar et al. (2024) created 20 reproducible tabletop scenes, each containing five objects from a set of 16 YCB objects. The robot attempts grasp, lift, rotate, transport, and drop-off. Both grasping success and complete pick-and-place success are scored separately over 100 object attempts per pipeline (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000069).

**Published results on Fetch robot.** Success rates ranged from 36% to 66% depending on the perception and grasp-planning pipeline. The best non-oracle result was GDRNPP + GraspIt! top-down grasping at 66/100 (66%). Ground-truth-pose variants reached 78–82/100 (pqac-00000066, pqac-00000067, pqac-00000068). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10610180 (peer-reviewed, ICRA 2024).

**Replication.** The YCB object set is commercially available. Scene layouts are specified with stencils. A low-cost arm with an RGB camera can replicate this, substituting its own perception pipeline.

---

### 7. ACRV Picking Benchmark

**Protocol.** Leitner et al. (2017) designed a reproducible shelf-picking benchmark with 42 common objects, a widely available shelf, and exact arrangement stencils. Four setups of increasing difficulty are each run three consecutive times. Success rate = successful picks / attempted picks (pqac-00000021). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2017.7989545 (peer-reviewed, ICRA 2017, 110 citations).

**Published results on Baxter.** Setup 1: 75% (9/12); Setup 2: 33.33% (4/12); Setup 3: 8.33% (1/12); Setup 4: 0% (0/18) (pqac-00000021).

**Replication.** The shelf and object arrangement are reproducible by design. A parallel gripper can substitute for the vacuum end-effector used on Baxter, though success rates will differ.

---

### 8. FMB — Functional Manipulation Benchmark

**Protocol.** Luo et al. (2024) proposed FMB using a Franka Panda with torque control. It evaluates grasping (5 trials × 10 objects = 50), single-object long-horizon manipulation (30 trials), and multi-object assembly (10 trials) using 66 reproducible 3D-printed objects. Observations include multi-camera RGB-D, kinematics, and force/torque (pqac-00000037, pqac-00000038).

**Published results.** Grasping: Transformer policy 28/50 (56%), ResNet 27/50 (54%). Single-object assembly: best 19/30. Multi-object assembly: best 7/10 (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000038). DOI: 10.1177/02783649241276017 (peer-reviewed, IJRR 2024, 161 citations).

**Replication.** The 3D-printed objects and CAD files are publicly available. A low-cost arm can attempt the grasping and single-object assembly tasks; multi-object assembly may require force sensing not available on budget platforms.

---

### 9. FurnitureBench

**Protocol.** Heo et al. (2025) evaluated long-horizon furniture assembly on a Franka Panda with the default parallel gripper and three Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D cameras. Eight 3D-printable furniture models test grasping, insertion, screwing, and pushing. Individual skills are evaluated over 10 trials under low/medium initialization randomness; termination occurs on completion, 5 s inactivity, unsafe motion, or step limits (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033). DOI: 10.1177/02783649241304789 (peer-reviewed, IJRR 2025, 241 citations).

**Published results.** Individual skill success rates vary by part and randomness. Full-assembly learning methods averaged at most 2 of 12 subtasks. Rebuilt environments achieved 84% of original one-leg-task phase performance (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034).

**Replication.** The 3D-printable models are available. Single-skill tasks (grasp, insert) are feasible on low-cost arms, though full assembly may exceed their capabilities.

---

### 10. Low-Cost Arm Benchmarks: SO-100/SO-101 with LeRobot

**SmolVLA on SO-100.** Shukor et al. (2025) evaluated ACT, SmolVLA, and π0 on three SO-100 tasks (pick-place, stacking, sorting) using 50 demonstrations per task. ACT achieved 70%/50%/25% (mean 48.3%); SmolVLA achieved 75%/90%/70% (mean 78.3%); π0 achieved 100%/40%/45% (mean 61.7%) (pqac-00000056, pqac-00000058). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2506.01844 (**preprint**, arXiv 2025, 655 citations).

**Cowling SO-101 scaling study.** Cowling (2026) compared ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0.5 on an SO-101 green-ball pick-and-place task with two distractors, using nested demonstration sets of 12–200. Each evaluation block ran 10 fixed placements with a 30 s timeout. Over 1,340 scored episodes, ACT improved from 1/40 at 12 demonstrations to 37/40 at 100; π0.5 achieved 16/40 at 12 and ~70% at higher counts; SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peaked near 50% (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.37170 (**preprint**, arXiv 2026).

**SO-101 Bench.** Hickok (2026) defined a language-conditioned spatial manipulation benchmark with Bin, Next-to, Between, and Move tasks across 916 simulated episodes and 60 paired physical episodes. Learned policies ranged from 8% to 60.8%; the best agent+grasp combination reached 83.2% in simulation (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031). DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.36420 (**preprint**, arXiv 2026).

---

### 11. Laboratory Manipulation Tasks

**MATTERIX.** Darvish et al. (2025) used a Franka Research 3 for lab tasks: beaker pick-and-place achieved 9/12 (75%) success; liquid pouring achieved 9/10 (90%) with 59.6 ± 7.9 mL transferred (pqac-00000055). DOI: 10.1038/s43588-025-00924-4 (peer-reviewed, Nature Computational Science 2025).

**Mobile robot rack handling.** Burger (2023) reported 464/464 (100%) rack transfers using a KUKA LBR iiwa arm with a Festo parallel gripper over 71 iterations in a 2-hour robustness test (pqac-00000050). DOI: 10.17638/03087073.

**ABB YuMi vial handling.** Manna et al. (2026) used an ABB YuMi IRB 14000 for end-to-end Drosophila vial handling, achieving 93.85% retention of flies fit for analysis across 1,024 assays versus 83.33% for a human (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000052). DOI: 10.64898/2026.10.20.758951 (**preprint**, bioRxiv 2026).

**No published evidence was found for a standardized, repeatable vial-into-rack insertion benchmark with trial-level success rates on any industrial arm.** This remains a gap in the literature.

---

### Summary and Gaps

The benchmarks most immediately replicable on a low-cost arm with a parallel gripper and RGB cameras are: (1) ISO 9283-style pose repeatability using AprilTag tracking in lieu of an OptiTrack system; (2) the Box and Blocks Test with the YCB apparatus; (3) YCB object pick-and-place following SceneReplica scenes; (4) NIST task board peg insertions (especially the larger pegs); (5) SO-100/SO-101 LeRobot tasks (pick-place, stacking, sorting), which are already native to the user's platform; and (6) the Van Wyk peg-in-hole protocol with 3D-printed artifacts.

**Explicit gaps.** No peer-reviewed ISO 9283 positional repeatability values were found for the AgileX PiPER or SO-101. No standardized vial-into-rack benchmark with published trial-level success rates exists. The QBIT and FMB force-based quality metrics require a force/torque sensor not present on budget arms. The Kinova Gen3 and ABB YuMi lack published results on the NIST task board or BBT benchmarks in the retrieved literature, limiting direct cross-arm comparisons for those specific platforms.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an ISO 9283-oriented robot repeatability protocol using both contact-based and vision-based measurements. Target poses were simulated in RoboDK, joint angles were extracted, and motions were programmed in Motion Perfect. In the vision tests, Phase 2a repeatedly moved between P1 and P2 with a mounted 4 kg payload, while Phase 2b evaluated five predefined positions (ISO P1–P5) forming the ISO 9283 cube. Every programmed position was executed 30 times; Phase 2b therefore involved 30 cycles per point. End-effector positions were recorded by a calibrated multi-camera vision system, exported as text files, cleaned in Excel, and analyzed in MATLAB. The reported repeatability metric was calculated as mean three-dimensional deviation plus three standard deviations (RPₗ = l̄ + 3σ). For the unloaded contact-based Phase 1 test, three orthogonal digital dial indicators and three cameras measured a spherical end-effector contacting a fixed point. After geometric sphere-center reconstruction, 30 trials produced a mean deviation of 0.0096 mm, standard deviation of 0.0055 mm, and final repeatability of 0.0260 mm. The excerpt does not report pose accuracy results, UR5, UR5e, Franka Panda, or other named robot comparisons, and it provides no DOI.

snippets: The ISO 9283 standard has emerged as the central reference, providing a structured and internationally accepted methodology for assessing and comparing the motion performance of different robotic systems.
Its emphasis on repeated motion cycles and statistical analysis ensures objective, reproducible results across varied testing scenarios.

Contact-based approaches—such as those involving mechanical dial indicators mounted in a three-axis fixture—offer extremely high measurement resolution and are particularly effective for evaluating static point-to-point repeatability.
In contrast, vision-based systems provide greater flexibility for tracking motion across larger workspaces and along dynamic trajectories.
In this thesis, both contact-based and vision-based measurement systems were applied to assess the repeatability performance of the RTA ARTIC6-1215-6kg robot.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the ISO 9283 protocol for evaluating industrial robot pose repeatability and accuracy. Pose repeatability concerns the robot’s ability to return to the same position and orientation, while pose accuracy is the deviation between commanded and actual positions. For repeatability, the robot is moved to a predefined target 30 times from the same approach direction, and the dispersion of the final positions is analyzed statistically using standard-deviation measures. Testing is performed at five workspace locations arranged as an ISO cube, allowing repeatability to be assessed spatially throughout the robot’s working volume. The excerpt discusses both contact-based and vision-based measurement. Contact-based setups use three orthogonally arranged digital dial indicators to detect deviations along X, Y, and Z, while the thesis’s modern system uses an optoelectronic vision system (OptiTrack) to reconstruct 3D coordinates from tracked markers. Vision systems support multi-point and trajectory measurements but require accurate calibration and can be affected by lighting, reflections, software accuracy, range, and occlusion. snippets: A subset of assembly tasks in the NIST Assembly Task Boards were selected as the benchmarking testbed, focusing on peg-in-hole type of operations
Specifically, 12 parts were chosen, ranging from round pegs to multi-pin connectors.
We mostly adopted the experimental protocol suggested in [9] and designed customized ﬁxtures to allow experiments to be reproducible and quantiﬁed.

For each of the 12 tasks, we implemented 3 solutions using OTS tools: 1) a position control baseline, 2) a hybrid motion/force control method (spiral search), and 3) a 3D vision-based pose estimation method.

The benchmarking experiments are further extended by introducing extra workspace variations to characterize the robustness of each method, including variations in task board presentation and external lighting.
Based on the empirical evaluation, we found the OTS tools are capable to solve most of the tasks, with different levels of generalization.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the NIST benchmarking protocol rather than reporting quantitative benchmark results for particular robot arms. It defines two test modes: disassembly and assembly. For assembly, a fully disassembled task board and parts kit are placed within the robot work volume; the robot autonomously grasps each part from the kit and assembles it onto the corresponding task-board destination, repeating this for all parts and for the desired number of trials. Board and kit positions may be fixed or randomized, with randomization intended to test perception, planning, and action. Multiple end-effectors and multiple robots are permitted, while manual system changes and manual or teleoperated intervention are not permitted. Performance is evaluated using completion time, board completion percentage, and reliability. Each board represents a subset of typical manufacturing assembly tasks and provides a defined procedure and scoring metric. The benchmark protocol consists of two phases: disassembly and assembly. For disassembly, a fully assembled board is placed within the robot’s workspace with an empty bin; the robot removes every component one at a time and places it in the bin, with the completion time recorded. For assembly, a fully disassembled board is placed alongside a task-specific kit-mat and any required feeder or binning mechanisms. The kit-mat specifies the starting location and orientation of each component. The robot grasps each part from the kit-mat and installs it into the board sequentially; each part is scored, and the total completion time is recorded. contexts.context: The excerpt describes the design and protocol scope of the NIST Assembly Task Boards, particularly Task Board 1, but it does not provide the requested quantitative benchmark results. Task Board 1 evaluates peg insertion, gear meshing, electrical connector insertion, and nut threading. Pegs vary in size and shape (round and rectangular), and a successful insertion requires the object to contact the surface below the board. Nut threading requires correct orientation and alignment, complete threading, and tightening to a specified torque. Gear meshing requires placing a gear on a shaft and meshing its teeth with an adjacent gear so that both gears rest completely on the base plate. Connector attachment is orientation-specific and requires insertion force; the BNC connector requires simultaneous pushing and twisting. The broader board design uses standard off-the-shelf components, with factors such as part size, symmetry, location, tool use, fixturing, resistance, visual occlusion, and obstruction incorporated into the tests. It does not identify connector-insertion or gear-meshing tasks, the robot arms used, success rates for individual tasks, or the total number of trials. It does describe ManipulationNet’s general benchmarking protocol, which may be relevant if the NIST benchmark was conducted under this infrastructure. Participants receive a standardized physical object set, configure their robotic system, and use an independent camera connected to the mnet-client. Trials are registered with the server and limited in number to reduce selection bias. During execution, a one-time submission code must remain visible, while the client reports task status and receives task instructions. The system records video, execution logs, and selected frames; lightweight metadata and cryptographic hashes are transmitted in real time rather than raw video. After completion, the full submission package is uploaded. The committee checks the code, hash consistency, and agreement between video content, duration, task status, and key frames before applying task-specific metrics. contexts.context: This excerpt describes the evaluation protocol and metric for the bin-picking benchmark, but it does not provide the requested quantitative success-rate results for specific physical robot arms such as Franka Panda, UR5, or Baxter. The benchmark evaluates multiple executions of predefined scenarios. In each execution, objects are placed in a storage container and the robot autonomously picks and places them one by one until the container is empty or the scenario’s maximum execution time is reached. The reported success rate is based on the number of objects successfully picked, transported, and placed (np) relative to the initial number of objects (n0), i.e., R = np/n0. Each pick-and-place cycle is classified by success or task-failure type; picking or placing multiple items in one cycle counts as a failure, and no external intervention is permitted. The excerpt also states that the benchmark can accommodate different sensing modalities, including tactile-only systems, and that the robot must detect when the container is empty. contexts.context: The excerpt reports SceneReplica physical pick-and-place benchmarking over 100 trials, consisting of 20 scenes with 5 objects per scene. Success is measured as the rate of transporting objects between locations, with separate grasping-success and pick-and-place-success figures. Failure analysis categorizes unsuccessful trials as perception, planning, or execution errors. Pose-estimation quality is evaluated using ADD-S, with a pose failure defined as ADD-S > 0.1 times the object diameter; segmentation is considered a failure when the F-measure is below 75%. In the reported table, model-based frameworks achieved pick-and-place success rates of 40–66/100 depending on method and grasping order; GDRNPP achieved 66/100 with near-to-far ordering and 62/100 with fixed ordering. Model-free frameworks achieved 36–61/100, with Contact-GraspNet generally outperforming GraspNet; the highest listed model-free result was 61/100 for MSMFormer plus Contact-GraspNet with fixed ordering. contexts.context: The excerpt reports a controlled LeRobot-based comparison on a low-cost SO-101 arm, not SO-100. The manipulation task was pick-and-place with two distractor objects. ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π0.5 were trained on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100, and 200 teleoperated demonstrations, using one fixed recipe per policy and several training seeds. Evaluation used ten fixed object placements, a 30-second episode limit, and 1,340 scored episodes organized into 126 blocks over 17 days. Success was assessed from recordings using a four-stage progression: starting movement, reaching the ball, carrying it, and delivering it; the excerpt does not explicitly define whether only delivery counted as overall success, but reports success counts per evaluation block. Quantitative examples include ACT improving from 1/40 successes with 12 demonstrations to 37/40 with 100; fine-tuned π0.5 achieving 16/40 at 12 demonstrations and 28/40 at 25, then approximately 70%; and SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peaking near 50%. Diffusion Policy often failed to initiate movement until idle lead-in frames were removed from demonstrations, while SmolVLA failed to start in 47% of episodes. The study emphasizes that results are specific to one task, arm, operator, and training recipe, with fixed training length confounding data quantity and exposure.

The scoring rewarded contact with target areas but penalized blocks partially off the printed template. The protocol used CBiRRT with TSR constraints and open-loop grasping and placement motions; success was limited by uncertainty, planning failures, and workspace-edge effects. In PR2 peg insertion learning, results were reported over 10 trials at each execution time: without perturbation, success increased from 7/10 at 0.5 seconds to 10/10 at 3 and 5 seconds. With 5 mm perturbation, success was 2/10, 4/10, 4/10, and 4/10; with 10 mm perturbation, it was 0/10 at all times. In the PR2 box-and-blocks test, ten two-minute experiments produced a mean of 7.3 successful transfers and 10.8 blocks transferred. The protocol repeatedly sampled pick locations, detected grasps by whether the gripper fully closed, and counted misses and transfer failures.

The primary SO-101 evaluation has 916 scored episodes across 15 task-family-by-object-split cells, covering bin placement, next-to, between, and move tasks, with seen, unseen-object/seen-class, and unseen-class objects. Success is determined automatically from simulator state: the relevant spatial condition must hold continuously for 5 seconds; episodes normally time out at 30 seconds, or 75 seconds for four-object bins. For spatial tasks, the target must move at least 1 inch, avoid end contact with the robot, and non-target objects must not move more than 1 inch. Training uses 3,629 teleoperated digital-twin episodes: 1,892 bin, 1,150 next-to/between, and 587 move episodes. Additional capability subsets include ROBUST (178 episodes), PLAN (48), and MEM (51). The excerpt also states that approximately 4,400 real-robot teleoperated episodes were released, but gives no corresponding real-robot success rates here.

FurnitureBench evaluates long-horizon furniture-assembly tasks involving grasping, re-orienting, inserting, and screwing. Its standardized setup uses a 7-DoF Franka Emika Panda arm with a default parallel gripper and three Intel RealSense D435 RGB-D cameras. The benchmark includes eight 3D-printed furniture models based on IKEA furniture, with task examples including chair and one-leg assembly. For reproducibility, ten participants independently built new environments from scratch; each setup took approximately three hours. A fully trained IQL-R3M policy was evaluated on the one_leg task in ten newly built environments. Under low randomness, the reproduced environments achieved an average of 84% of the performance of the original environment, measured by completed subtasks or phases. contexts.context: The excerpt reports quantitative FMB results for hierarchical and non-hierarchical policies, but it does not identify the robot arm used. Evaluations include single-object manipulation and multi-object, multi-stage assembly tasks involving an assembly board; grasping and insertion are discussed as component skills. For single-object tasks, hierarchical methods reached 19/30 and 15/30 with Transformer-based policies, while a conditioned ResNet achieved 0/30 and chaining separate policies achieved 18/30. For multi-object tasks evaluated on the red assembly board, the conditioned hierarchical Transformer achieved 7/10 successes and the conditioned hierarchical ResNet achieved 5/10; unconditioned policies achieved 0 successes. The excerpt characterizes 30 trials as the evaluation size for the single-object results and 10 trials for the multi-object assembly results. It also notes that insertion performed best with three RGB camera views, while adding a fourth view could hurt ResNet performance when the board position was randomized. Overall, the reported best results are 19/30 for single-object tasks and 7/10 for multi-object tasks, despite using a human oracle as the high-level policy.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports benchmark details for a UR5e-based 3DVision system, using a customized gripper and two LMI 3506 Gocators. For each insertion task, 150 trials were conducted; the system achieved a 100% task completion rate except for four RJ45 failures. Its practical tolerance area was constrained by the camera field of view: 22 mm in x, 33 mm in y, and 18 mm in z. The excerpt also describes position and force-based benchmarking across 12 insertion tasks. Force increased the combined succeeded-and-possible tolerance area for all peg types, with especially strong improvement for round pegs. Among connectors, USB had the lowest tolerance because of its small dimensions and sharp edges, while RJ45 had the largest tolerance because of clearance between the connector and socket; waterproof connectors also had a large tolerance area. The protocol used separate coarse-benchmarking and validation boards to reduce wear-and-tear effects, and aluminum boards were used instead of the plexiglass boards from the original NIST Assembly Task Board #1. However, this excerpt does not state specific clearance values, peg diameters, insertion completion times, or detailed NIST peg-insertion results by robot arm.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes the peg-in-hole benchmark design and performance measures but does not report the numerical results for specific robot arms or the NIST Assembly Task Board peg-insertion results. The test uses 3-D-printable pegs and holes with a dimensionless clearance of c = (D − d)/D = 0.02. Each test begins with two pegs in two holes and involves cyclic transfer into the next available hole. Positional offsets are deliberately introduced in X and Y, sampled from zero-mean Gaussian distributions with standard deviations of 1 mm and 2 mm. The same positional-error sequence is applied to both systems. The experiment includes 60 attempted insertions. Performance is evaluated using completion time (CT), defined as the time required to align and successfully insert the peg; peg acquisition and transport are excluded. It also uses probability of success (PS), calculated from the number of samples and successes with a 95% confidence level. contexts.context: The excerpt reports quantitative results for a collaborative robot cell performing automated Drosophila vial handling and sex classification, but it does not identify the robot as a Franka Panda, UR5, or ABB YuMi, nor does it provide separate success rates for rack insertion or pipetting. The protocol begins with the robot picking up an adult-fly vial, anesthetizing it with a CO2 needle, and opening it over a vibrating sieve so flies are distributed onto a CO2 pad. A DSLR camera acquires one 6000 × 4000 pixel image; computer vision detects flies, identifies males using body shape and posterior abdominal pigmentation, and transfers coordinates to the robot for sex-based handling. Against human-determined ground truth, robotic sex classification achieved 92.3% accuracy over 350 flies in 12 images. The full robotic procedure took approximately 40 seconds per vial: about 20 seconds for vial handling, 20 seconds for image acquisition, and 200 milliseconds for classification. The comparison manual protocol required 9 ± 3 minutes per vial containing 70–120 flies, based on 20 vials. Thus, the reported measurements are classification accuracy against human labels and timed workflow components, rather than independent arm-manipulation success rates or trial counts for rack insertion/pipetting.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports quantitative results for STELA, a standard dual-arm collaborative robot used to automate an established Drosophila operant-conditioning experiment. It does not identify the robot as a Franka Panda, UR5, or ABB YuMi, and it does not provide separate success rates or trial counts specifically for vial handling, rack insertion, pipetting, or individual manipulation subtasks. At the whole-workflow level, STELA completed 16 consecutive experiments and 1,024 individual visual-learning assays during a 24-hour cycle, whereas a human completed 6 experiments and 384 assays during 8 hours. The proportion of flies retained as fit for analysis was 93.85% for the robot versus 83.33% for the human, and robotic handling consistency improved 12-fold. The protocol included vial handling, CO2 anaesthesia, machine-vision sex classification, vision-guided transfer of individual flies, behavioural-arena loading, assay initiation, and post-assay recovery. Measurement involved counting completed experiments and assays, assessing the percentage of recovered flies suitable for analysis, and comparing handling consistency and behavioural outcomes between biologically matched robotic and manual experiments. The excerpt states that robotic and manual handling produced the same mean behavioural outcomes while reducing inter-individual variability, but it does not describe the exact consistency metric or provide per-task trial-level success rates.

snippets: We design four categories of tabletop manipulation tasks for the SO100 setup: (1) Pick&Place: involving 3 objects and 2 placement zones (6 tasks), (2) MoveTo: navigating 2 objects to a single target zone (2 tasks), (3) Wipe: picking up a cloth and wiping the table (1 task), and (4) Unfold: unfolding a cloth (1 task).

During evaluation, each task is tested over 10 trials, and success rates are reported.

We have a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. Examples: ISO 9283 pose repeatability and accuracy, repeated pick-and-place success over N trials, peg-in-hole, NIST task boards, YCB object protocols, and lab tasks such as vial and rack handling.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. We have a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. Repeatable benchmarks: Which published manipulation benchmarks with quantitative results for industrial or research arms could be rerun on a low-cost arm with a parallel gripper and RGB cameras? Examples: ISO 9283 pose repeatability and accuracy, repeated pick-and-place success over N trials, peg-in-hole, NIST task boards, YCB object protocols, and lab tasks such as vial and rack handling.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We have a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and compare them with industrial and research arms (e.g. UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) using tests we can repeat ourselves.

Repeatable benchmarks: Which published manipulation benchmarks with quantitative results for industrial or research arms could be rerun on a low-cost arm with a parallel gripper and RGB cameras? Examples: ISO 9283 pose repeatability and accuracy, repeated pick-and-place success over N trials, peg-in-hole, NIST task boards, YCB object protocols, and lab tasks such as vial and rack handling.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


## Repeatable Manipulation Benchmarks for Comparing Low-Cost and Industrial/Research Robot Arms

This report identifies published manipulation benchmarks with quantitative results obtained on industrial or research arms that could be rerun on a low-cost 6-DOF arm (such as AgileX PiPER or SO-101) equipped with a parallel gripper and RGB cameras. For each benchmark, the protocol, trial count, success criterion, measuring tool, arm model, and key quantitative result are described. The following table provides a comprehensive summary of all identified benchmarks.

| Benchmark Name | Category | Robot Arm(s) Tested | Protocol Summary | Trials/Cycles | Success Metric | Key Quantitative Result | Sensor/Measuring Tool | DOI | Publication Type |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|---|---|---|---|
| ISO 9283 pose repeatability | Metrology | RTA ARTIC6-1215-6kg; related ISO-inspired tactile study tested Franka Emika Panda, UR5e, UR10e | Approach each target repeatedly from the same direction; measure terminal Cartesian positions at five ISO-cube points. Compute positional repeatability as mean radial deviation plus three standard deviations. Test unloaded and with payload. | 30 approaches per target | Position repeatability, mm; optionally pose accuracy as commanded-versus-mean-measured pose | ARTIC6: unloaded contact test 0.0260 mm; 4 kg vision test 0.0406 mm; five-point results 0.02691–0.26279 mm. No peer-reviewed ISO 9283 positional result for PiPER or SO-101 was found. (nasertorabi2024repeatabilityassessmentof pages 24-26, nasertorabi2024repeatabilityassessmentof pages 1-4, nasertorabi2024repeatabilityassessmentof pages 7-10) | Three orthogonal digital dial indicators and spherical tool; calibrated OptiTrack multi-camera system | No DOI for the ARTIC6 thesis; related UR5 paper: [10.1177/1687814020972893](https://doi.org/10.1177/1687814020972893); tactile study: [10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329](https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329) | Thesis/non-peer-reviewed quantitative source; related peer-reviewed journal and IROS paper |
| Box and Blocks Test: Modified, Targeted, Standard | Cluttered pick-and-place | Franka Emika Panda; Barrett WAM | Use YCB Box-and-Blocks apparatus. Modified: transfer 16 aligned blocks over barrier. Targeted: add ordered/accurate placement. Standard: move as many randomly arranged blocks as possible; timed version lasts 60 s. Run each protocol consecutively at least five times; failed executions score zero. | At least 5 runs per protocol | Blocks transferred or ordered-placement score; attempts, path length, planning, execution and total time | Panda averages: Modified score 14.4, 247.94 s; Targeted score 13.0, 307.10 s; timed Standard 2.8 blocks/60 s; untimed Standard 7.6 blocks in 248.73 s. (morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 5-6, morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 2-3, morgan2020benchmarkingclutteredrobot pages 4-5) | Intel RealSense D435i eye-in-hand RGB-D on Panda; Kinect point cloud on WAM; manual/video scoring and controller logs | [10.1109/LRA.2019.2961053](https://doi.org/10.1109/LRA.2019.2961053) | Peer-reviewed journal, IEEE RA-L 2020 |
| NIST Assembly Task Board 1: peg insertion | Precision assembly | UR5e in the off-the-shelf benchmark | Pick from a nest board and insert four round pegs (4, 8, 12, 16 mm) and four rectangular pegs into an aluminum validation board. Compare position control, hybrid motion/force spiral search and 3-D vision; inspect insertion outcome. NIST defines success as the peg contacting the surface below the board. | 150 trials per insertion task for the UR5e 3-D-vision evaluation | Completion proportion; tolerance region; cycle time | The 3-D-vision system completed all peg tasks in the reported 150-trial-per-task evaluation; the paper reports 100% for all 12 tasks except four RJ45 failures. Individual peg cycle times were not separately published. (lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 4-5, lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 2-3, kimble2020benchmarkingprotocolsfor pages 3-5) | Two LMI Gocator 3506 3-D sensors; customized gripper; optional force feedback; operator inspection | [10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636586](https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636586); protocol: [10.1109/LRA.2020.2965869](https://doi.org/10.1109/LRA.2020.2965869) | Peer-reviewed IROS 2021 paper; peer-reviewed RA-L protocol |
| NIST Assembly Task Board 1: connector insertion | Connector assembly | UR5e | Insert USB, RJ45, waterproof and DSUB connectors after grasping from fixed nests. Use pose estimation and insertion control; release, retract and inspect. Repeat under board-presentation and lighting variations. | 150 trials per task for 3-D-vision test; end-to-end table’s denominator not stated in retrieved text | Successful fully seated connector; mean cycle time | End-to-end completion/time: USB 100%/29.8 s; RJ45 96%/33.6 s; waterproof 98%/30.1 s; DSUB 100%/28.0 s. The 3-D-vision study had four RJ45 failures and otherwise 100% completion. (lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 7-7, lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions pages 4-5, lian2021benchmarkingofftheshelfsolutions media c9397f47) | LMI Gocator 3506 sensors; custom gripper; optional force feedback; operator inspection | [10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636586](https://doi.org/10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636586) | Peer-reviewed major conference, IROS 2021 |
| YCB SceneReplica | Replicable cluttered pick-and-place | Fetch mobile manipulator; benchmark generation also illustrates Franka Panda | Recreate 20 tabletop scenes, each containing five objects selected from 16 YCB objects. Attempt grasp, lift, rotate/transport and drop-off; report grasp success separately from complete pick-and-place success. | 100 object attempts per pipeline: 20 scenes × 5 objects | Complete pick-and-place success count/100 | Published pipelines achieved 36–66% complete pick-and-place; best reported non-ground-truth result was GDRNPP + GraspIt! top-down + near-to-far ordering at 66/100. Ground-truth-pose variants reached 78–82/100. (khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 9-11, khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 6-7, khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 5-6, khargonkar2024scenereplicabenchmarkingrealworld pages 3-5) | Robot RGB-D camera; perception/grasp pipeline; benchmark scene geometry | [10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10610180](https://doi.org/10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10610180) | Peer-reviewed major conference, ICRA 2024 |
